items.title: Focus Question: What properties distinguish a fluid from a solid, and how do gases and liquids differ from each other?

body.html: Compare how particles are arranged and how they move in each state.

answer.html: A fluid is a material that flows and has no shape of its own, so it takes the shape of its container; liquids and gases are fluids. A liquid has a definite volume and is nearly incompressible, because its particles touch. A gas fills any container and is easily compressed, because its particles are far apart. Both exert pressure, and warming either one makes it less dense so that it rises.

items.title: Figure 1, Identify: A hot-air balloon floats above a field. What fluid surrounds the balloon, and what fluid fills the balloon?

body.html: The balloon is surrounded by the atmosphere, and its envelope is filled with heated air.

answer.html: The balloon is surrounded by air (a gas, mostly nitrogen and oxygen). Inside it is also air, but heated, so it is less dense than the outside air.

items.title: Pressure section, Calculate: A Mars lander weighs 8,400 N on the surface of Mars and rests on three circular footpads, each 0.75 m in diameter. (a) Find the pressure it exerts on the ground. (b) Estimate the pressure from a suited astronaut standing on the surface, stating your assumptions.

body.html: Weight 𝐹= 8, 400 N; three circular pads, each of diameter 𝑑= 0.75 m, so 𝑟= 0.375 m. Find the pressure on the ground, then estimate the astronaut's pressure.
Pressure is force divided by contact area, 𝑃= 𝐹/ 𝐴. The lander's weight is spread over the area of all three pads.
Find the area of one circular pad, then of three.

For the astronaut, assume a total mass (person plus suit) of 150 kg. On Mars 𝑔≈3.71 m/s<sup>2</sup>, so the weight is about (150)(3.71) = 557 N. Assume two boot soles of about 0.025 m<sup>2</sup> each, so 𝐴≈0.050 m<sup>2</sup>. Then:

answer.html: (a) The lander presses on the ground with about 6.3 kPa. (b) The astronaut (assuming about 150 kg and 0.050 m² of boot area) presses with about 1 × 10<sup>4</sup> Pa, roughly twice as much as the lander.

check.html: Both pressures are only a few kPa to 10 kPa, far below one atmosphere on Earth, so neither sinks deeply into the soil.

items.title: CCC: Structure and Function, make a model that shows how the properties of liquids and gases come from their particle structure (use a drop of water and the air around it)

body.html: Particle spacing, motion and attractions explain what a fluid does.

Draw a labeled two-panel particle diagram. Gas (air around the drop): particles far apart and moving fast with almost no attraction, so the air has no definite shape or volume, fills any container, can be compressed, and exerts pressure through collisions. Liquid (the water drop): particles touching but able to slide past one another, so the water flows, has a definite volume, takes the shape of its container (or a rounded drop shape when free), and resists compression.

answer.html: Neither liquid nor gas particles are locked in fixed positions, so both flow. Widely spaced gas particles explain compressibility and low density. Close-packed, sliding liquid particles explain a fixed volume and flow.

items.title: Practice Problem 1: Atmospheric pressure is 1.0 × 105 Pa. Find the force of the air on the top of a table that measures 1.83 m by 0.91 m.

body.html: 𝑃= 1.0 × 10<sup>5</sup> Pa; table 1.83 m × 0.91 m. Find 𝐹.
𝑃= 𝐹/ 𝐴, so 𝐹= 𝑃𝐴.
Find the area, then the force.

answer.html: 1.7 × 10<sup>5</sup> N (straight down on the top surface)

check.html: This is about 37,000 lb. The table does not collapse because air pushes up on the underside with an equal force.

items.title: Practice Problem 2: A 1350-kg car rests on four tires. Each tire has a contact patch of 13 cm by 19 cm. Find the pressure of the tires on the road.

body.html: Four patches, each 13 cm × 19 cm; 𝑚= 1350 kg. Find 𝑃.
The weight is the force, 𝐹= 𝑚𝑔, and it is spread over the total contact area, 𝑃= 𝐹/ 𝐴.

check.html: A little more than one atmosphere, which is in the normal range of tire pressures.

items.title: Practice Problem 3: An iron block measures 4.0 cm by 8.0 cm by 25.0 cm and has a density of 7.87 g/cm³. It rests on its smallest face (4.0 cm by 8.0 cm). Find the pressure on the table.

body.html: Block 4.0 cm × 8.0 cm × 25.0 cm, 𝜌= 7.87 g/cm<sup>3</sup>, resting on its smallest face. Find 𝑃.
Find the mass from density times volume, then the weight, then divide by the contact area.

answer.html: 1.9 × 10<sup>4</sup> Pa (19 kPa)

check.html: The smallest face gives the largest pressure, as it should.

items.title: Practice Problem 4: During a hurricane the outside air pressure drops 12% below its normal value of 1.0 × 105 Pa, while the pressure inside a sealed room stays the same. Find the net force on a window that is 1.40 m by 0.85 m, and its direction.

body.html: Outside pressure is 12% below 1.0 × 10<sup>5</sup> Pa; window 1.40 m × 0.85 m. Find the net force and its direction.
Inside the room the pressure stays at its original value, so the net force comes from the pressure difference, 𝐹= 𝛥𝑃𝐴.

answer.html: 1.4 × 10<sup>4</sup> N, directed outward (from the higher inside pressure toward the lower outside pressure)

check.html: About 3,200 lb of outward force, which explains why windows can blow out when the pressure drops quickly.

items.title: Practice Problem 5 (Challenge): A 620-kg machine must rest on a steel plate on a floor that can safely carry an added pressure of only 4.0 × 104 Pa. What is the smallest area the plate can have?

body.html: 𝑚= 620 kg; allowed pressure 𝑃= 4.0 × 10<sup>4</sup> Pa. Find the minimum plate area 𝐴.
𝑃= 𝐹/ 𝐴 with 𝐹= 𝑚𝑔, so 𝐴= 𝑚𝑔/ 𝑃 is the minimum area.

answer.html: At least 0.15 m<sup>2</sup> (for example, about 39 cm × 39 cm)

check.html: A bigger area lowers the pressure, as intended. The plate's own weight is neglected.

items.title: Figure 4, Explain: A sealed, rigid metal can of gas is cooled in a freezer. What happens to the gas pressure, and why?

body.html: With 𝑉<sub>1</sub> = 𝑉<sub>2</sub> the combined gas law becomes 𝑃<sub>1</sub> / 𝑇<sub>1</sub> = 𝑃<sub>2</sub> / 𝑇<sub>2</sub> (Gay-Lussac's law).

The can is rigid, so the volume cannot change. Colder gas particles move more slowly, so they hit the walls less often and less hard. The pressure falls in direct proportion to the Kelvin temperature.

answer.html: The pressure decreases. At constant volume, pressure is directly proportional to Kelvin temperature: <sup>𝑃</sup><sup>1</sup> <sup>𝑇</sup><sub>1</sub> =<sup> </sup><sup>𝑃</sup><sup>2</sup>

items.title: Practice Problem 6: A 0.035 m³ tank holds neon at 12.0 × 10⁶ Pa and 288 K. The gas is released into a balloon at 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa and 303 K. Find the volume of the balloon.

body.html: 𝑃<sub>1</sub> = 12.0 × 10<sup>6</sup> Pa, 𝑉<sub>1</sub> = 0.035 m<sup>3</sup>, 𝑇<sub>1</sub> = 288 K; 𝑃<sub>2</sub> = 1.01 × 10<sup>5</sup> Pa, 𝑇<sub>2</sub> = 303 K. Find 𝑉<sub>2</sub>.
A fixed amount of gas changes pressure, volume and temperature, so use the combined gas law, <sup>𝑃</sup><sup>1</sup><sup>𝑉</sup><sup>1</sup>
<sup>𝑇</sup><sub>2</sub> .
Rearrange for 𝑉<sub>2</sub>, then substitute.

answer.html: 4.4 m<sup>3</sup>

check.html: The pressure falls by a factor of about 120 while the temperature rises a little, so the volume rises by about 120 times: 0.035 × 120 ≈4.2. Reasonable.

items.title: 20.2 g/mol.

body.html: 𝑃= 12.0 × 10<sup>6</sup> Pa, 𝑉= 0.035 m<sup>3</sup>, 𝑇= 288 K, 𝑀= 20.2 g/mol. Find 𝑚.
Use 𝑃𝑉= 𝑛𝑅𝑇 to find the number of moles, then multiply by the molar mass.

check.html: A 35-L tank at about 120 atm holds about 175 mol, and each mole of neon is about 20 g, so about 3.5 kg.

items.title: Practice Problem 8: A tank holds 150.0 L of oxygen at 5.0°C and 182 kPa. The gas is heated to 80.0°C and the tank's volume is changed to 130 L. Find the new pressure.

body.html: 𝑉<sub>1</sub> = 150.0 L, 𝑇<sub>1</sub> = 5.0°C = 278 K, 𝑃<sub>1</sub> = 182 kPa; 𝑇<sub>2</sub> = 80.0°C = 353 K, 𝑉<sub>2</sub> = 130 L. Find 𝑃<sub>2</sub>.
Combined gas law (the amount of gas is fixed). Convert temperatures to kelvins first. The volumes can stay in liters because they appear as a ratio.

answer.html: 2.67 × 10<sup>2</sup> kPa

check.html: A hotter gas and a smaller volume both raise the pressure, so 𝑃<sub>2</sub> > 𝑃<sub>1</sub>.

items.title: Practice Problem 9 (Challenge): Find the volume of 2.0 kg of nitrogen gas (molar mass 28 g/mol) at 25.0°C and 1.013 × 105 Pa.

body.html: Convert mass to moles, then use 𝑃𝑉= 𝑛𝑅𝑇.
𝑉= 𝑛𝑅𝑇

answer.html: 1.7 m<sup>3</sup>

check.html: Nitrogen has a density of about 1.15 kg/m<sup>3</sup> at this temperature, so 2.0 kg occupies about 1.7 m<sup>3</sup>. It matches.

items.title: Check Your Progress 10: A neon sign tube, a glass of juice and the air in a bicycle tire all contain fluids. Compare and contrast the gas, the liquid and the plasma in these objects.

body.html: A lit neon sign contains a plasma (ionized gas), the juice is a liquid and the tire holds a gas. Compare what the particles are doing. Property Juice (liquid) Tire air (gas) Lit neon tube (plasma) Shape Takes shape of container Takes shape of container Takes shape of the tube Volume Definite Fills whole container Fills whole tube Particle spacing Close together, sliding Far apart, fast Far apart, ionized Property Juice (liquid) Tire air (gas) Lit neon tube (plasma) Compressibility Very small Large Large Electrical conduction Poor (pure liquid) Insulates Conducts and glows

answer.html: All three can flow and take the shape of their container. The liquid has a definite volume and is nearly incompressible. The gas and the plasma expand to fill their containers. The plasma differs from the gas because its atoms are ionized, so it conducts electricity and gives off light in the tube.

items.title: Check Your Progress 11: Two boxes, one 15 cm by 15 cm by 15 cm and one 15 cm by 15 cm by 45 cm, hang from the ceiling of a room. (a) Compare the air pressure on the outside of each box. (b) Compare the total force the air exerts on each.

body.html: Boxes of 15 × 15 × 15 cm and 15 × 15 × 45 cm. (a) Compare air pressures. (b) Compare total forces.

Air pressure depends on the air (its altitude and temperature), not on the shape of an object. Force is 𝐹= 𝑃𝐴, so it depends on the surface area. Both boxes hang at about the same height, so the pressure is the same on both. Work (b): Compute the surface areas.

The longer box has about 2.3 times the surface area, so the air presses on it with about 2.3 times the total force in magnitude. The forces on opposite faces point in opposite directions, so the net force from the air on each box is nearly zero (a tiny buoyant force).

answer.html: (a) The pressure is the same on both boxes. (b) The longer box feels about 2.3 times the total force magnitude, in proportion to its surface area (the net force is about zero for both).

check.html: Pressure does not depend on size (same), while force scales with area.

items.title: Check Your Progress 12: A research balloon holds 18.0 m³ of gas at ground level, where the pressure is 1.01 × 105 Pa. It rises to a height where the pressure is 0.74 × 105 Pa. If the temperature does not change, find its new volume.

body.html: 𝑉<sub>1</sub> = 18.0 m<sup>3</sup> at 𝑃<sub>1</sub> = 1.01 × 10<sup>5</sup> Pa; 𝑃<sub>2</sub> = 0.74 × 10<sup>5</sup> Pa; 𝑇 constant. Find 𝑉<sub>2</sub>.
Constant temperature means Boyle's law, 𝑃<sub>1</sub>𝑉<sub>1</sub> = 𝑃<sub>2</sub>𝑉<sub>2</sub>.

answer.html: 25 m<sup>3</sup>

check.html: Lower pressure means a larger volume. Correct direction.

items.title: Check Your Progress 13: How does the density of water change when it is cooled (a) from 10°C to 6°C, and (b) from 10°C to 1°C?

body.html: Water is densest at 4°C. Above 4°C it behaves normally, so cooling contracts it and raises its density. Below 4°C the ice-like structure begins to open up, so water expands and its density falls as it cools toward 0°C. Work (a): 10°C to 6°C stays above 4°C, so the water contracts and its density increases. Work (b): 10°C to 4°C is an increase in density, then 4°C to 1°C is a decrease. The final density is below the maximum.

answer.html: (a) The density increases. (b) The density first increases (to its maximum at 4°C) and then decreases between 4°C and 1°C.

items.title: of 3.6 × 106 Pa. Find the temperature of the compressed air.

body.html: 𝑉<sub>1</sub> = 0.0016 m<sup>3</sup>, 𝑃<sub>1</sub> = 1.013 × 10<sup>5</sup> Pa, 𝑇<sub>1</sub> = 285 K; 𝑃<sub>2</sub> = 3.6 × 10<sup>6</sup> Pa, 𝑉<sub>2</sub> = 0.00009 m<sup>3</sup>. Find 𝑇<sub>2</sub>.
Combined gas law, solved for 𝑇<sub>2</sub>.

answer.html: about 6 × 10<sup>2</sup> K (about 570 K before rounding to the one significant figure of 0.00009 m<sup>3</sup>)

check.html: Fast compression heats the air a great deal, to hundreds of degrees above room temperature. Reasonable.

items.title: Check Your Progress 15: What volume does 2.50 mol of an ideal gas occupy at 298 K and

body.html: Ideal gas law, 𝑉= 𝑛𝑅𝑇/ 𝑃.

answer.html: 6.11 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>2</sup> m<sup>3</sup> = 61.1 L

check.html: One mole occupies about 24.5 L at 298 K, and 2.5 × 24.5 = 61 L. It matches.

items.title: Check Your Progress 16: A walk-in freezer has a volume of 1.20 m³ and a temperature of -18°C at a pressure of 1.013 × 105 Pa. Find the number of moles and the mass of the air inside. The molar mass of air is 29 g/mol.

body.html: 𝑉= 1.20 m<sup>3</sup>, 𝑇= −18°C = 255 K, 𝑃= 1.013 × 10<sup>5</sup> Pa, 𝑀= 29 g/mol. Find 𝑛 and 𝑚.
𝑃𝑉= 𝑛𝑅𝑇 for 𝑛, then 𝑚= 𝑀𝑛.

check.html: 1.20 m<sup>3</sup> of cold air at about 1.4 kg/m<sup>3</sup> is about 1.7 kg. It matches.

items.title: Check Your Progress 17: Critical thinking. A 1.5-L container of nitrogen and a 1.5-L container of argon are at the same pressure and temperature. Which contains more particles, and which has more mass?

body.html: In an ideal gas, 𝑃𝑉= 𝑛𝑅𝑇 contains no term for the size or kind of particle. The particles are treated as points that take up almost no space.
Equal 𝑃, 𝑉 and 𝑇 give equal 𝑛 (and equal 𝑁). The mass is 𝑚= 𝑛𝑀, with 𝑀<sup>N</sup><sub>2</sub> = 28 g/mol and 𝑀<sup>Ar</sup> = 40 g/mol.

answer.html: Both containers hold the same number of particles. The argon has the greater mass, because each argon atom is more massive than a nitrogen molecule (40 versus 28 in molar mass units).

items.title: Focus Question: What is a fluid and what are its properties?

body.html: Compare what the lesson says about liquids, gases and plasma.

answer.html: A fluid is a material that can flow and has no definite shape of its own (liquids and gases). Its properties include pressure (force per area, exerted in all directions), compressibility (large for gases, small for liquids), and thermal expansion, which makes warm fluid less dense so that it rises.

items.title: Figure 1, Identify: What fluid fills the space above the water?

body.html: The lake is surrounded by the atmosphere.

answer.html: Air (a gas), which includes some water vapor from evaporation.

items.title: Pressure section, Calculate: the lunar module and the astronaut

body.html: Weight 𝐹= 12, 000 N; four circular pads, each of diameter 𝑑= 91 cm = 0.91 m. Find the pressure on the Moon's surface, and estimate the astronaut's pressure.
Pressure is force divided by contact area, 𝑃= 𝐹/ 𝐴. The module's weight is spread over the area of all four pads.
Find the area of one circular pad, then of four.

For the astronaut, estimate the weight and the boot area. A suited astronaut might have a mass of about 180 kg. On the Moon (𝑔≈1.62 m/s<sup>2</sup>) the weight is about (180)(1.62) = 290 N. Two boot soles of about 0.03 m<sup>2</sup> each give 𝐴≈0.06 m<sup>2</sup>. Then:

answer.html: The lunar module exerts about 4.6 kPa. The astronaut is estimated (using stated assumptions: about 180 kg, about 0.06 m² of boot area) at about 5 kPa, similar to the module.

check.html: Both are only a few kPa, far below atmospheric pressure, which is why the lander does not sink far into the lunar soil.

items.title: CCC: Structure and Function, make a model that the properties of fluids come from their molecular structure

body.html: Particle arrangement and attractions explain what a fluid does.

A model can be a labeled particle diagram with three panels. Gas: particles are far apart and move fast with almost no attraction, so a gas has no definite shape or volume, fills any container, is compressible, and exerts pressure through collisions with the walls. Liquid: particles are touching but slide past one another, so a liquid flows, takes the shape of its container, has a definite volume, and is hard to compress. Plasma: a gas hot enough to knock electrons off atoms, giving free charges, so it flows like a gas but also conducts electricity.

answer.html: Because liquid and gas particles are not locked in fixed positions, both flow and take the shape of their containers. Gas particles are far apart (compressible, low density); liquid particles are close (nearly incompressible).

items.title: Practice Problem 1: Force of air on a desk top

body.html: 𝑃= 1.0 × 10<sup>5</sup> Pa; desk 1.52 m × 0.76 m. Find 𝐹.
𝑃= 𝐹/ 𝐴, so 𝐹= 𝑃𝐴.
Find the area, then the force.

answer.html: 1.2 × 10<sup>5</sup> N (straight down on the top surface)

check.html: About 26,000 lb of force. The desk does not collapse because air pushes up on the underside with an equal force.

items.title: Practice Problem 2: Pressure of a car on the ground

body.html: Four tires, each with contact area 12 cm × 18 cm; 𝑚= 925 kg. Find 𝑃.
The weight is the force, 𝐹= 𝑚𝑔, spread over the total contact area, 𝑃= 𝐹/ 𝐴.

check.html: About one atmosphere, which matches tire-inflation pressures seen in practice.

items.title: Practice Problem 3: Pressure of a lead brick

body.html: Brick 5.0 cm × 10.0 cm × 20.0 cm, 𝜌= 11.8 g/cm<sup>3</sup>, resting on its smallest face (5.0 cm × 10.0 cm). Find 𝑃.
Find the mass from density times volume, then weight, then divide by the contact area.

answer.html: 2.3 × 10<sup>4</sup> Pa (23 kPa)

check.html: The smallest face gives the largest pressure, as it should.

items.title: Practice Problem 4: Door during a storm

body.html: Outside pressure drops 15% below 1.0 × 10<sup>5</sup> Pa; door 1.95 m × 0.91 m. Find the net force and its direction.
Inside the house the pressure stays at the original value, so the net force comes from the pressure difference, 𝐹= 𝛥𝑃𝐴.

answer.html: 2.7 × 10<sup>4</sup> N, directed outward (from the higher inside pressure toward the lower outside pressure)

check.html: A force of about 6,000 lb on a door explains why a rapid pressure drop can blow doors and windows out.

items.title: Practice Problem 5 (Challenge): Size of the steel support plate

body.html: 𝑚= 454 kg; allowed added pressure 𝑃= 5.0 × 10<sup>4</sup> Pa. Find the plate area 𝐴.
𝑃= 𝐹/ 𝐴 with 𝐹= 𝑚𝑔, so 𝐴= 𝑚𝑔/ 𝑃 is the minimum area.

answer.html: At least 0.089 m<sup>2</sup> (for example, about 30 cm × 30 cm)

check.html: A bigger area lowers the pressure, as intended. The plate's own weight is neglected.

items.title: Figure 4, Explain: What happens if you hold volume constant?

body.html: With 𝑉<sub>1</sub> = 𝑉<sub>2</sub> the combined gas law becomes 𝑃<sub>1</sub> / 𝑇<sub>1</sub> = 𝑃<sub>2</sub> / 𝑇<sub>2</sub> (Gay-Lussac's law, as the figure shows).
At fixed volume, hotter gas particles move faster and hit the walls harder and more often, so the pressure rises in direct proportion to the Kelvin temperature.

answer.html: Pressure is directly proportional to Kelvin temperature: <sup>𝑃</sup><sup>1</sup>

items.title: Practice Problem 6: Helium balloon from a tank

body.html: 𝑃<sub>1</sub> = 15.5 × 10<sup>6</sup> Pa, 𝑉<sub>1</sub> = 0.020 m<sup>3</sup>, 𝑇<sub>1</sub> = 293 K; 𝑃<sub>2</sub> = 1.00 atm = 1.01 × 10<sup>5</sup> Pa, 𝑇<sub>2</sub> = 323 K. Find 𝑉<sub>2</sub>.
A fixed amount of gas changes pressure, volume and temperature, so use the combined gas law.
Rearrange for 𝑉<sub>2</sub>, then substitute.

answer.html: 3.4 m<sup>3</sup>

items.title: Practice Problem 7: Mass of the helium

body.html: Use the tank data: 𝑃= 15.5 × 10<sup>6</sup> Pa, 𝑉= 0.020 m<sup>3</sup>, 𝑇= 293 K, 𝑀= 4.00 g/mol. Find 𝑚.
Use 𝑃𝑉= 𝑛𝑅𝑇 to find the number of moles, then multiply by the molar mass.

body.html: 𝑉<sub>1</sub> = 200.0 L, 𝑇<sub>1</sub> = 0.0°C = 273 K, 𝑃<sub>1</sub> = 156 kPa; 𝑇<sub>2</sub> = 95°C = 368 K, 𝑉<sub>2</sub> = 175 L. Find 𝑃<sub>2</sub>.
Combined gas law (the amount of gas is fixed). Convert temperatures to kelvins first. The volumes can stay in liters because they appear as a ratio.

answer.html: 2.40 × 10<sup>2</sup> kPa

check.html: Both a hotter gas and a smaller volume raise the pressure, so 𝑃<sub>2</sub> > 𝑃<sub>1</sub>.

items.title: Practice Problem 9 (Challenge): Volume of 1.0 kg of air

body.html: Convert mass to moles, then use 𝑃𝑉= 𝑛𝑅𝑇.
𝑉= 𝑛𝑅𝑇

answer.html: 0.83 m<sup>3</sup>

check.html: Air has a density of about 1.2 kg/m<sup>3</sup>, so 1 kg occupies about 0.83 m<sup>3</sup>. It matches.

items.title: Check Your Progress 10: Compare and contrast liquids, gases and plasmas

body.html: Compare what each state's particles are doing. Property Liquid Gas Plasma Shape Takes shape of container Takes shape of container Takes shape of container Volume Definite Fills whole container Fills whole container Particle spacing Close together, sliding Far apart, fast Far apart, ionized Compressibility Very small Large Large Electrical conduction Poor (pure liquids) Insulates Conducts, can glow

answer.html: All three can flow and have no shape of their own. Liquids have a definite volume and are nearly incompressible; gases and plasmas expand to fill their containers. Plasma differs from a gas because its atoms are ionized, so it conducts electricity and responds to electric and magnetic fields.

items.title: Check Your Progress 11: Two boxes hung in air

body.html: Boxes of 20 × 20 × 20 cm and 20 × 20 × 40 cm. (a) Compare the air pressure on the outside. (b) Compare the total force of the air.

Air pressure depends on the air (its altitude and temperature), not on the shape of the object. Force is 𝐹= 𝑃𝐴, so it depends on the surface area. The two boxes are at essentially the same height and neither is on the ground, so the air pressure is the same for both. Work (b): Compute the surface areas, using 𝑃 for the same air pressure.

The second box has about 1.7 times the surface area, so air presses on it with about 1.7 times as much total force (in magnitude). The air forces on opposite faces point in opposite directions, so the net force from the air on each box is nearly zero (a tiny buoyant force).

answer.html: (a) The pressure is the same on both boxes. (b) The larger box feels about 1.7 times the total force magnitude, in proportion to its surface area (the net force is about zero for both).

check.html: Pressure is intensive (same), force is extensive (scales with area).

items.title: Check Your Progress 12: Weather balloon

body.html: 𝑉<sub>1</sub> = 25.0 m<sup>3</sup> at sea level (𝑃<sub>1</sub> = 1.01 × 10<sup>5</sup> Pa); 𝑃<sub>2</sub> = 0.82 × 10<sup>5</sup> Pa; 𝑇 constant. Find 𝑉<sub>2</sub>.
Constant temperature means Boyle's law, 𝑃<sub>1</sub>𝑉<sub>1</sub> = 𝑃<sub>2</sub>𝑉<sub>2</sub>.

answer.html: 31 m<sup>3</sup>

check.html: Lower pressure means a larger volume. Correct direction.

items.title: Check Your Progress 13: Density of water from 0°C

body.html: From 0°C to 4°C, water contracts as ice crystals collapse, so its volume decreases and the density increases. Water is densest at 4°C. Above 4°C, ordinary thermal expansion takes over and the density decreases.
From 0°C to 4°C the density rises to its maximum. From 4°C to 8°C the water expands normally, so the density falls again from that maximum.

answer.html: 0°C to 4°C: the density increases (to its maximum at 4°C). 4°C to 8°C: the density decreases.

items.title: Check Your Progress 14: Engine compression

body.html: 𝑉<sub>1</sub> = 0.0021 m<sup>3</sup>, 𝑃<sub>1</sub> = 1.013 × 10<sup>5</sup> Pa, 𝑇<sub>1</sub> = 303 K; 𝑃<sub>2</sub> = 20.1 × 10<sup>5</sup> Pa, 𝑉<sub>2</sub> = 0.0003 m<sup>3</sup>. Find 𝑇<sub>2</sub>.
Combined gas law, solved for 𝑇<sub>2</sub>.

answer.html: about 9 × 10<sup>2</sup> K (about 860 K before rounding to the one significant figure of 0.0003 m<sup>3</sup>)

check.html: Rapid compression heats the air a great deal, enough to ignite diesel fuel. Reasonable.

items.title: Check Your Progress 15: Standard molar volume

body.html: Ideal gas law, 𝑉= 𝑛𝑅𝑇/ 𝑃.

answer.html: 2.24 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>2</sup> m<sup>3</sup> = 22.4 L

check.html: This is the well-known value of 22.4 L per mole at standard conditions.

items.title: Check Your Progress 16: Air in a refrigerator

body.html: 𝑉= 0.635 m<sup>3</sup>, 𝑇= 2.00°C = 275 K, 𝑃= 1.013 × 10<sup>5</sup> Pa, 𝑀= 29 g/mol. Find 𝑛 and 𝑚.
𝑃𝑉= 𝑛𝑅𝑇 for 𝑛, then 𝑚= 𝑀𝑛.

check.html: 0.635 m<sup>3</sup> of cold air at about 1.3 kg/m<sup>3</sup> is about 0.8 kg. It matches.

items.title: Check Your Progress 17: Critical thinking, CO₂ vs helium

body.html: In an ideal gas, 𝑃𝑉= 𝑛𝑅𝑇 (or 𝑃𝑉= 𝑘𝑁𝑇) contains no term for the size or kind of particle. The particles are treated as points that take up almost no space (the gas is mostly empty space).
Same 𝑃, 𝑉 and 𝑇 give the same 𝑁, no matter how large the individual particles are.

answer.html: The two 2.0-L samples contain the same number of particles (Avogadro's idea), even though the CO₂ molecules are larger and more massive. The CO₂ sample has the greater mass.
